planting.note: Start seed indoors 10-8 weeks before the last frost, since Prizetaker needs a long season to reach its full exhibition size; transplant once the soil can be worked.

directions: Prizetaker is a long-day Spanish-type heirloom introduced by W. Atlee Burpee and Co. in 1888 and prized for producing some of the largest bulbs of any yellow onion, often reaching a pound or more under good conditions. The globe-shaped bulbs have thin golden-brown skin over mild, sweet, white flesh well suited to fresh eating, slicing, and frying rather than long storage. Grow in deeply worked, fertile soil with steady moisture through bulb swell, since the variety's size depends on an uninterrupted growing season. Harvest once tops fall over and cure briefly before use, as the high moisture content of this sweet type limits how long it keeps.
sources: W. Atlee Burpee and Co. historical catalog records
Mother Earth News heirloom onion variety guide

common_name: Barletta Onion (Early Italian Pearl Pickling Onion)

planting.note: Direct-sow thickly around the last frost; Barletta matures very quickly into pearl-sized bulbs and can be succession-sown for a continuous supply of small pickling onions.

directions: Barletta is a short-day Italian heirloom grown for its small, smooth, round-to-flattened white bulbs, typically harvested at only three-quarters of an inch to one inch across for use as pickled cocktail onions. Because the variety matures so quickly, it is usually direct-sown and grown at tight spacing so the crowded bulbs stay small rather than sizing up into full storage onions. The thin white skin and crisp, mild flesh make it a classic choice for traditional pickled pearl onions as well as kabobs and quick-cooked dishes. Lift the whole crop while bulbs are still young and tender, since Barletta's flavor and texture are best before the papery skins toughen.

common_name: Early Yellow Globe Onion (1930s American Long-Day Heirloom)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant as soon as soil is workable; Early Yellow Globe is a long-day type suited to the Mid-Atlantic and northern growing regions.

directions: Early Yellow Globe is an American long-day heirloom introduced around 1930 and long maintained by commercial growers in New York's Orange County before entering heirloom seed networks. It forms a medium-sized, flattened-globe bulb of about two and a half to three inches with light yellow skin and firm, mildly pungent flesh suited to both cooking and winter storage. The variety is noted for resisting pink root, a common soil-borne onion disease, which has helped it remain in cultivation in the regions where that pressure is high. Start early, since its earlier maturity compared to full-season storage onions makes it a reliable choice where the growing season runs short.

common_name: North Holland Blood Red Onion (Noordhollandse Bloedrode)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once soil is workable; this long-day Dutch heirloom needs a full season to size up its large flattened bulbs.

directions: North Holland Blood Red is a long-day Dutch heirloom valued for its large, slightly flattened bulbs covered in shiny, deep ox-blood red skin. The pungent flesh is layered with red and white rings and mellows noticeably with storage, making mature bulbs milder than fresh-pulled ones. This variety has a long history of supplying Dutch markets through winter, reflecting its exceptional keeping quality compared to most red onions. Harvest once tops fall over and cure thoroughly in a dry, airy spot before storing in a cool location for extended use.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange international variety records

common_name: Bianca di Maggio Onion (Italian White Cipollini)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Bianca di Maggio is a long-day Italian cipollini type that can also be pulled young as a sweet spring onion.

directions: Bianca di Maggio is an Italian heirloom cipollini onion forming petite, saucer-shaped bulbs with papery white skin and translucent white flesh, distinguished from the more familiar golden Borettana cipollini by its pale coloring. The flavor is firm, semi-sweet, and mildly pungent when raw, and the flattened shape makes bulbs especially convenient for grilling whole on skewers or kabobs. Harvested young, it serves as a tender spring onion; left to mature, the bulbs develop good storage life for a cipollini type. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil with even moisture, since the shallow, wide bulbs are more prone to drying out than deep-rooted globe onions.

common_name: Chet's Italian Red Garlic (Pacific Northwest Softneck Heirloom)

planting.note: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep, in fall 2-4 weeks before the ground freezes; as a softneck, Chet's Italian Red does not need as long a cold period as hardneck types.

directions: Chet's Italian Red is a softneck artichoke-type garlic discovered growing in an abandoned garden near Tonasket, Washington, in the 1960s and reselected for decades before entering wider cultivation. Bulbs form in overlapping clove layers, typically yielding ten to twenty cloves under milk-white to pale yellow skin, with a mild flavor that gains more heat when grown in colder climates than its Pacific Northwest origin. As a softneck, it produces no flower scape and its flexible stems can be braided for storage. Harvest when the lower leaves begin to brown, cure in a shaded, airy spot for several weeks, and expect good keeping quality of up to about six months.
